prompt: A sequence reads x y x y x y. What is the shortest unit that repeats?
optionC: x
optionD: x y x
explanation: Two symbols repeat three times, and no shorter unit does. The four-symbol unit repeats too, which is why the question asks for the shortest.

prompt: A sequence reads p q r p q r p q r. Which unit, repeated, produces it, taken as short as possible?
optionA: p q r p q r
optionC: p
optionD: p q r
explanation: Three symbols repeat throughout. A two-symbol unit fits the opening and then fails, which is the shape of a unit inferred from the start alone.

prompt: This sequence is built by repeating a single unit: a a b a a b a a b. Taken as short as it can be, what is that unit?
optionC: a a
optionD: a a b a a b
explanation: The unit a a b is three symbols long and includes the doubled opening symbol. Taking a b instead would produce a b a b, which is not what is shown.

prompt: A sequence reads m n n m n n m n n. How long is the shortest repeating unit?
optionC: Three symbols
optionD: One symbol
explanation: The sequence is built from m n n repeated three times, so the shortest unit is Three symbols long. Six symbols also repeat, being twice the shortest unit rather than the unit itself.

prompt: A sequence reads d e d e d e d. Does it have a repeating unit, and if so what is it?
optionA: No; the sequence does not divide evenly into units
optionB: Yes, d e; the sequence stops part way through a repetition
optionC: Yes, d e d; the last symbol proves the unit is three long
optionD: Yes, d; every symbol is either d or e
correctAnswerText: Yes, d e; the sequence stops part way through a repetition
explanation: A pattern may be cut short without ceasing to be a pattern, so ending mid-unit changes nothing. Reading the trailing d as evidence of a three-symbol unit contradicts the rest of the sequence.

prompt: Is the arrangement a b c b a symmetric, and about what?
optionA: No; the symbols are not all the same
optionC: No; a symmetric arrangement must have an even number of symbols
optionD: Yes, about its middle symbol
explanation: Reading it from either end gives the same sequence, with c at the centre. An odd count is perfectly compatible with symmetry — it simply leaves one symbol in the middle.

prompt: Is the arrangement p q p q symmetric?
optionA: No; reading it backwards gives q p q p
optionC: Yes; it is symmetric about the gap in the middle
optionD: Yes; both halves contain the same symbols
correctAnswerText: No; reading it backwards gives q p q p
explanation: Repetition and symmetry are different properties, and this arrangement has the first without the second. Containing the same symbols in each half is not the same as reading alike in both directions.

prompt: Is the arrangement w x y x w symmetric?
optionA: No; the middle symbol has no partner
optionB: No; five symbols cannot be symmetric
optionC: Yes; the first and last match, and so do the second and fourth
optionD: Yes; every symbol appears twice
correctAnswerText: Yes; the first and last match, and so do the second and fourth
explanation: Symmetry requires each symbol to match its partner counting inward from the ends, and the middle symbol needs none. The symbol y appears once, which is exactly what a centre looks like.

prompt: An arrangement reads r s t s r except that one position has been changed, giving r s t r r. Is it still symmetric?
optionB: No; the fourth position no longer matches the second
optionC: Yes; only one position changed
optionD: No; symmetry requires all symbols to differ
correctAnswerText: No; the fourth position no longer matches the second
explanation: Symmetry has to hold at every pair, so a single mismatched position breaks it however much of the rest survives. The ends matching is necessary and not sufficient.

prompt: An arrangement a b c becomes c b a. Which transformation is that?
optionC: No transformation; the two are the same
optionD: A mirror
explanation: A mirror is what reverses the order. A shift would move every symbol along and bring one round to the other end, which gives a different result.

prompt: An arrangement a b c d becomes d a b c. Which transformation is that?
optionA: A shift, with the last symbol brought to the front
optionC: A swap of the two ends
optionD: A sort into reverse order
correctAnswerText: A shift, with the last symbol brought to the front
explanation: Every symbol has moved one place along and the one that fell off the end has come round. Mirroring would have given d c b a, which is not what is shown.

prompt: An arrangement a b c d becomes a c b d. Which transformation is that?
optionC: A swap of the two middle symbols
optionD: A half-turn
correctAnswerText: A swap of the two middle symbols
explanation: A swap of the two middle symbols is all that has happened: only those two moved, and they exchanged places. A mirror or a shift would have moved the outer symbols too.

prompt: Someone says an arrangement was mirrored, and someone else says it was given a half-turn. The arrangement is a b b a and both descriptions produce it. What follows?
optionA: One of the two must be wrong
optionB: The two cannot be told apart on this input, because it is symmetric
optionC: A mirror and a half-turn are the same transformation
optionD: The arrangement was not transformed at all
correctAnswerText: The two cannot be told apart on this input, because it is symmetric
explanation: Two different transformations agree on an input that is already symmetric, so this input cannot distinguish them. Testing on an arrangement that is not symmetric is what would settle it.

prompt: A sequence repeats the unit triangle circle, beginning triangle circle triangle circle triangle. What comes next?
optionC: The sequence ends here
optionD: circle
explanation: Five symbols have been shown and the unit is two long, so the sixth completes the third repetition. Nothing new enters a repeating sequence.

prompt: A sequence repeats the unit a b c. What is at position 10, counting the first symbol as position 0?
optionC: c
optionD: It cannot be found without writing the sequence out
explanation: Position 10 divided by the unit length of 3 leaves a remainder of 1, and the symbol at that place in the unit is b . Counting from one instead would give a, which is the neighbouring answer.

prompt: Four arrangements: a a b, m m n, p p q, r s s. Which has a different structure?
optionC: r s s
optionD: p p q
explanation: Three of them double the first symbol and end with a different one; the fourth doubles the second. The letters differ throughout, so only the structure can decide it.

prompt: Four arrangements: x y x, k l k, d e d, f g h. Which has a different structure?
optionC: k l k
optionD: d e d
explanation: Three arrangements return to their opening symbol and one does not. Every arrangement uses different letters, so content cannot be the discriminator.

prompt: On a two-by-two grid with positions named top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left, one mark sits at top-left. After a quarter turn clockwise, where is it?
optionC: Top-left, unchanged
optionD: Top-right
explanation: A quarter turn clockwise moves each corner to the next one round in that direction. Answering bottom-left turns it the other way.

prompt: On the same grid, marks sit at top-left and bottom-right. After a quarter turn clockwise, where are they?
optionC: Bottom-left and top-right, which is a quarter turn the other way
optionD: Top-left and bottom-left
explanation: Each mark moves to the next corner clockwise, so the pair moves from one diagonal to the other. The second and third options name the same pair of corners, which is why the direction has to be reasoned about rather than recognised.

prompt: A mark at top-left is given a quarter turn clockwise, then another, then another. Someone says three quarter turns leave it where it started. Where is it in fact?
optionC: Bottom-left
optionD: Bottom-right
explanation: Three quarter turns is a three-quarter turn, which lands one corner short of a full circle. Four would return it to the start, which is what the claim confuses it with.

prompt: A row reads a b c d. It is mirrored about a vertical line down its middle. What does it read afterwards?
optionC: b a d c
optionD: d a b c
explanation: Mirroring about a vertical line exchanges the ends and works inward, reversing the order to give d c b a . Exchanging only adjacent pairs would give b a d c.

prompt: On a two-by-two grid a mark sits at top-left. It is mirrored about a vertical line down the middle. Where is it?
optionC: Top-left, unchanged
optionD: Top-right
explanation: A vertical mirror exchanges left and right and leaves top and bottom alone. Answering bottom-left mirrors about a horizontal line instead.

prompt: An arrangement is mirrored about a vertical line, and the result is mirrored about the same line again. Someone expects a different arrangement each time. What is the final result?
optionC: An arrangement mirrored about a horizontal line
optionD: An arrangement turned by a quarter
explanation: Mirroring twice about the same line undoes itself, whatever the arrangement was. Expecting each transformation to change things again treats the operations as accumulating when they cancel.

prompt: Facing north, a person turns right. Which direction are they now facing?
optionC: East
optionD: North
explanation: A right turn from north faces east. Answering west turns the other way, and south would need two turns.

prompt: Starting at a point, a marker moves 3 steps east and then 2 steps west. Where is it relative to where it began?
optionC: 1 step west
optionD: Back where it began
explanation: Movements in opposite directions partly cancel, leaving the difference. Adding both distances together ignores the directions entirely.

prompt: Facing north, a marker moves 2 steps forward, turns right, and moves 2 steps forward. Someone says it has moved 4 steps north. The turn happens between the two moves. Where is it?
optionC: Back where it began
optionD: 2 steps north and 2 steps east of where it began
correctAnswerText: 2 steps north and 2 steps east of where it began
explanation: The turn changes what "forward" means, so the two moves go in different directions. Summing the distances without accounting for the turn is exactly the error the claim makes.

prompt: A sequence reads a a b b a a b b. It has an inner pattern of doubled symbols and an outer pattern alternating between a and b. What comes next?
optionC: a a
optionD: b b
explanation: The doubled b has just completed, so the outer pattern moves on to a and its first copy comes next. Answering b continues the inner doubling one step too far.

prompt: A sequence reads x y y x y y x. The outer pattern places an x and the inner pattern follows it with two y symbols. What are the next two?
optionC: y y
optionD: x x
explanation: An x has just been placed, so the inner pattern supplies its two y symbols before the outer pattern comes round again. Continuing the outer pattern first applies the two rules in the wrong order.

prompt: A sequence reads p q q r p q q r. Someone continues it as p q q r p q q r p, which continues the outer pattern. The question asks what comes next at the inner level. What is the answer?
optionB: q, because the inner pattern follows each p with two q symbols
optionC: r, because the unit ends with r
optionD: Nothing; the inner pattern has no next element
correctAnswerText: q, because the inner pattern follows each p with two q symbols
explanation: Two patterns are running at once, and the question names which one it is asking about. Continuing the outer pattern is a correct answer to a different question, which is what makes reading the question part of the work.

prompt: Three arrangements: a b a, c d c, e f e. What structural rule do they all satisfy?
optionA: They all contain the letters a, b and c
optionB: They are all three symbols long
optionC: They all begin with a vowel
optionD: The first and third symbols are the same and the middle one differs
correctAnswerText: The first and third symbols are the same and the middle one differs
explanation: The rule has to hold for every arrangement and describe the arrangement rather than its contents. Being three symbols long is true and too weak to distinguish them from anything else of that length.

prompt: Three arrangements: m m n p, k k l q, r r s t. What structural rule do they all satisfy?
optionA: The first symbol is doubled, and the remaining two differ from it and from each other
optionB: They all begin with a consonant
optionC: The first two symbols are the same
optionD: They are all four symbols long
correctAnswerText: The first symbol is doubled, and the remaining two differ from it and from each other
explanation: Saying only that the first two match is true and misses that the last two are distinct, which is also common to all three. A rule that is true and incomplete describes more arrangements than the ones shown.

prompt: Three arrangements: a b b a, m n n m, x y y x. Someone states the rule as "the first and last symbols match". That is true of all three. Why is it not the best statement of the rule?
optionA: It is false for one of the three
optionB: It is stronger than the arrangements support
optionC: It is weaker than the arrangements support; the middle pair also matches, and the arrangements are fully symmetric
optionD: It describes the content rather than the structure
correctAnswerText: It is weaker than the arrangements support; the middle pair also matches, and the arrangements are fully symmetric
explanation: The proposed rule holds and admits arrangements the examples do not include, such as a b c a. Stating the strongest rule the examples support is what makes it a description of these arrangements rather than of a wider family.

prompt: Items are described by shape and size: small circle, large circle, small square, large square, small circle. What comes next?
optionC: Large square
optionD: Small circle
explanation: The size alternates small and large on every item while the shape changes every two items, and the sequence has just returned to its start. Each wrong option continues one attribute and freezes or misreads the other.

prompt: Items vary in colour and count: one red, two blue, three red, four blue, five red. Someone answers six red, continuing the count and freezing the colour. Both attributes follow their own rule. What comes next?
optionC: Seven blue
optionD: Six blue
explanation: The count rises by one each time and the colour alternates, so both move together. Freezing one attribute while advancing the other is the commonest way a two-attribute pattern is misread.

prompt: A growing arrangement has 1 element at stage 1, 3 at stage 2, 5 at stage 3 and 7 at stage 4. How many at stage 10?
explanation: Each stage adds two, so the count is twice the stage number less one, giving 19 at stage 10. Answering 9 reports the stage-5 count, and 17 stops one stage short.

prompt: A growing arrangement has 2 elements at stage 1, 6 at stage 2, 12 at stage 3 and 20 at stage 4. Someone continues by adding the last increment of 8 again. The increments are 4, 6 and 8, which themselves grow. How many elements at stage 6?
explanation: The increments rise by two each time, so stage 5 adds 10 and stage 6 adds 12, giving 30 and then 42. Reusing the last increment gives 28, which is what continuing by the difference rather than by the rule produces.

prompt: A sequence built from the unit a b c reads a b c a b c a c c a b c. Where is the break, and what should be there?
optionA: The ninth symbol, which should be b
optionB: The eighth symbol, which should be b rather than c
optionC: The seventh symbol, which should be b
optionD: The last symbol, which should be a
correctAnswerText: The eighth symbol, which should be b rather than c
explanation: The unit repeats cleanly except in the third repetition, where the middle symbol is wrong. Naming the position after the break is the commonest slip, because that is where the sequence first looks unfamiliar.

prompt: A sequence reads m n m n m m m n m n. Someone identifies the last symbol as the break, on the grounds that it is where they stopped reading. The rule is inferable from the unbroken part alone. Where is the break?
optionA: The last symbol, as they said
optionB: The fifth symbol, which should be n
optionC: The seventh symbol, which should be n
optionD: The sixth symbol, which should be n rather than m
correctAnswerText: The sixth symbol, which should be n rather than m
explanation: The unit m n repeats throughout except for one extra m in the middle, and the sequence resumes correctly afterwards. Suspecting the end by default is a habit worth resisting, since the closing symbols here fit perfectly.

prompt: A sequence contains exactly one break. Two different rules each fit the unbroken part, and they disagree about which symbol is the break. What follows?
optionA: The break cannot be located until the rule is settled, and the sequence shown does not settle it
optionB: Whichever rule is simpler identifies the true break
optionC: Both breaks are genuine, since both rules fit
optionD: The sequence contains no break after all
correctAnswerText: The break cannot be located until the rule is settled, and the sequence shown does not settle it
explanation: A break is a deviation from a rule, so it has no location until the rule is fixed. Two rules fitting equally well is exactly the situation where more of the sequence is needed rather than a preference between them.

prompt: A sequence has a break at its very first symbol. Why is that harder to detect than a break in the middle?
optionA: A break at the start is not a break at all
optionB: The first symbol has no predecessor to compare with
optionC: The rule is inferred from what is read first, so a wrong opening symbol is taken as part of the rule
optionD: It is not harder; every position is equally visible
correctAnswerText: The rule is inferred from what is read first, so a wrong opening symbol is taken as part of the rule
explanation: Reading a sequence builds an expectation from its opening, so a fault there is absorbed into the expectation rather than measured against it. The lack of a predecessor is a real point and not the reason — a break in the second symbol has a predecessor and is also easy to absorb.

prompt: A long sequence contains one break. Checking every position takes time; checking only where the sequence "looks wrong" is quick. What does the quick approach risk?
optionA: Nothing; a break is always visible where it occurs
optionB: Missing a break that the reader's own expectation has absorbed, and stopping at a position that merely follows the break
optionC: Finding too many breaks rather than too few
optionD: Taking longer than checking every position
correctAnswerText: Missing a break that the reader's own expectation has absorbed, and stopping at a position that merely follows the break
explanation: Where a sequence looks wrong is often one position after where it went wrong, and a break the reader has already fitted into their rule never looks wrong at all. The quick approach is often right and its failures are systematic rather than random.

prompt: An arrangement of letters reads a b b a. Which arrangement of numbers shares its structure? The content shares nothing with the original.
explanation: The structure is first and last matching with a matched pair inside, and only one option has it. Each other option is a plausible four-item arrangement with a different structure.

prompt: A sequence of colours reads red red blue. Which sequence of words shares its structure?
optionC: up down up
optionD: up up up
explanation: The structure is a doubled first item followed by a different one, and only one option matches it. Recognising a structure across entirely different content is what makes it a structure rather than a description of the items.

prompt: A sequence of sizes reads small large small large. Which of these shares its structure?
optionC: A sequence of numbers reading 2 9 2 9
optionD: A sequence of sizes reading small small large large
explanation: The structure is two items alternating, and only one option alternates. The last option shares the original's content entirely and has a different structure, which is exactly the trap.

prompt: Two arrangements share a structure. Does that mean they will behave the same way when the same rule is applied to each?
optionB: Yes for any rule that depends only on the structure, and not for one that depends on the content
optionC: No; sharing a structure says nothing about behaviour
optionD: Yes, provided the two use the same kind of item
correctAnswerText: Yes for any rule that depends only on the structure, and not for one that depends on the content
explanation: A rule about positions and repetitions sees only the structure and treats the two identically. A rule that asks which item is larger, or which comes first alphabetically, reaches past the structure into the content.

prompt: Recognising structure across different content is useful and can mislead. When does it mislead?
optionA: Never; shared structure always means shared behaviour
optionB: Whenever the two contents are of different kinds
optionC: Whenever the arrangements have different lengths
optionD: When the shared structure is superficial and the content is what the problem actually turns on
correctAnswerText: When the shared structure is superficial and the content is what the problem actually turns on
explanation: Seeing that two problems have the same shape is what lets a solution transfer, and it fails exactly when the shape was not the important thing. Different kinds of content and different lengths are not themselves obstacles.

prompt: A sequence reads a b a b. It fits both "a and b alternating" and "the unit a b repeated". Someone says the two are different structures that happen to agree. What would distinguish them?
optionA: Nothing; on this kind of sequence the two descriptions are the same structure in different words
optionB: A longer sequence would separate them
optionC: A sequence starting with b would separate them
optionD: The two disagree from the fifth symbol onward
correctAnswerText: Nothing; on this kind of sequence the two descriptions are the same structure in different words
explanation: Alternating two symbols and repeating a two-symbol unit describe identical sequences, so no continuation can separate them. Recognising that two descriptions are one structure is as useful as separating two that genuinely differ.

prompt: A sequence reads a b b a. It fits both "symmetric about its middle" and "the unit a b followed by that unit mirrored". What continuation would distinguish the two?
optionB: A shorter sequence would distinguish them
optionC: A longer sequence: symmetry constrains the whole arrangement, while a mirrored-unit rule predicts a b b a a b b a
optionD: Changing the letters would distinguish them
correctAnswerText: A longer sequence: symmetry constrains the whole arrangement, while a mirrored-unit rule predicts a b b a a b b a
explanation: The two agree on what has been shown and make different predictions about what follows, so the continuation is where they part. Changing the content leaves both structures intact and settles nothing.

prompt: Two structures fit an arrangement, and one is much simpler to state. Is simplicity a reason to prefer it?
optionA: Yes; the simpler structure is always the real one
optionB: It is a practical preference and not evidence; only an observation the two disagree about settles it
optionC: No; the more detailed structure explains more and is better
optionD: Yes; a simpler structure is easier to test
correctAnswerText: It is a practical preference and not evidence; only an observation the two disagree about settles it
explanation: Simplicity makes a structure easier to state and to use, and neither of those makes it the one behind the arrangement. What decides between two structures is a case they predict differently.

prompt: Someone proposes extending an arrangement to test which of two structures holds, and chooses an extension both structures predict. What has the test achieved?
optionB: It has confirmed the simpler structure
optionC: It has ruled out any third structure
optionD: Nothing; an observation both structures predict cannot tell them apart
correctAnswerText: Nothing; an observation both structures predict cannot tell them apart
explanation: A test is informative only where the competing explanations disagree, and this one was chosen where they agree. It is the same reasoning as choosing a test input that a correct and a faulty program would answer identically.
